newsitem.title: UK: International LPG weak in East Asia, strong in N S.
newsitem.headline: International LPG weak in East Asia, strong in N S.

text.p: International Liquefied Petroleum Gas (LPG) prices were mixed this week, with propane prices rallying strongly in northwest Europe but levels in East Asia falling as the unchanged Saudi Contract Price (CP) failed to stir up buying interest.

Fluctuating crude and naphtha prices sent propane prices in the North Sea first down then up, a Scandinavian trader said. And he added that with crude dropping again at the end of the week, there was likely to be a downturn in propane prices again.

The rise in propane in northwest Europe was due to a combination of factors of which the crude price was only one, he said. As important was the fact that a lot of propane was moved into cavern storage the previous week as players have started building up relatively low-priced stocks ahead of next winter, he said.
"It's physically driven. There's no big petrochemical demand, it's the higher oil price and storage that's done it," he said.

Propane sellers were heard asking as high as $190 a tonne cif northwest Europe by the end of the week, with buyers having to come up to the mid-$180's a tonne. But the spike was expected to be short lived. "It won't last long unless more tonnes are dedicated to storage," a trader said.

But with the propane price still high at least for the short term, sellers of Algerian material were keeping an eye on the market to consider whether it may be worth moving material north. A seller of Algerian tonnes said that the US remained the market of choice for Algerian propane, but added they were considering opportunities in northern Europe. He added that the local Mediterranean market remained thin.

But butane in northwest Europe weakened over the week, with a trader assessing the value of large cargoes at $170 a tonne cif NWE. "Butane should be more of an indicator of value for the petrochemical side," he said. He added that the weakness of butane confirmed the view that the strength of propane owed more to storage buying than to petrochemical demand.
The spot markets in the Middle East Gulf and East Asia remained subdued. A Japanese trader said that Japanese buyers remained "sidelined" as the market is getting weaker.

"The market is getting weaker," he said. "How weak is the next question. If the weakness continues, buyers will come to the market slowly." But he added that if prices started to pick up, there could be a rush as buyers will conclude that prices have bottomed out and are set to carry on rising for the rest of the year.

The CP, the benchmark against which most trade in Asian markets is priced, was unchanged from June to July, but the trader said this had not given a clear signal to the market on whether prices have now reached the bottom. Players are already trying to gauge the level of the August CP, he said, but for now premiums to the July CP have started to soften.

A mixed propane/butane cargo was reported traded in the range CP + $14 to $16 a tonne C+F South Korea towards the end of the week. The C+F Japan price is seen as around $2 a tonne higher than the Korean price. So sellers are now heard offering around CP + $20 C+F Japan, compared with previous business done at around CP + $25.

Freight from the Middle East Gulf to Japan is seen at around $30 a tonne, so a level of CP +$20 C+F Japan should net back to around CP - $10 fob Gulf, a trader said. In fact, a small propane piece was heard traded at CP -$6.00 or -$6.50 a tonne fob Saudi Arabia, and buyers are back down to CP -$10 a tonne, he said.

On the most recent Saudi spot tender, the July T3 tender, it was reported that propane was not awarded and butane was awarded at close to $190 a tonne. The first August T1 tender closes on Friday, with bids valid until July 8. It will be for 8.5 kt to 12.5 kt of both propane and butane for loading August 1 to 11.
